title: Cora and Maple's Apple Surprise
markdown:
Beside a meadow that shimmered like a green velvet blanket lived two squirrels named Cora and Maple. Cora, eyes like shiny acorns that twinkled with thoughtfulness, had a careful tail that twitched when she was pondering. Maple, her cheerful friend, had a tail as fluffy and warm as a dandelion puff, always ready for a happy wiggle. Every day, as the morning mist lifted, they scampered down to Mr. Thistlewick’s fruit stand. Apples piled high in glorious round pyramids, cheeks rosy and gleaming, smelled so sweet.

Cora, with neat little paws, loved to make sure each apple sat just so, arranging them with care, tail a quiver of satisfaction. Maple helped too, tail wagging a happy rhythm as she placed the round sweet fruits. Together they built grand apple towers, tall and proud, and when they were finished they stood back, proud of their beautiful pointy pyramids. Quiet peaceful work, like a soft lullaby for squirrel hearts. Every day the same gentle dance of stacking and admiring, a ritual as comforting as the sunrise. The apples gleamed under the kind sun, and the pyramids grew taller and grander, each one a testament to patient efforts. They loved the feeling of order, of things being just right, just so.

Until one day, when the sun was beginning to dip, painting the sky orange and rose, a very special visitor arrived. Coach Pansy, a wise old rabbit whose long soft ears often drooped when she was deep in thought, eyes holding a gentle knowing like a quiet pond. She ambled to the stand, nose twitching as if smelling the stories the air carried. “Good day, little ones,” she whispered, voice like dry leaves in a breeze. “I shall take just one apple, if you please. One that whispers of sunshine and laughter.”

Eager to please, they presented their finest pyramid, the one that reached highest. Coach Pansy looked at the very top apple, round and perfect. Then the next one down, and the next, gaze soft. She reached out a delicate paw and, with the gentlest touch, lifted the apple from the second row, right in the middle. The whole pyramid seemed to let out a tiny surprised sigh. It wobbled just a little, as if taking a deep breath, and the neat straight rows suddenly looked a little untidy. Apples on top leaned this way and that. The grand structure seemed to reconsider its perfect shape. Cora’s neat whiskers drooped. Maple let out a tiny questioning chirp. Who could have guessed that one apple could make such a gentle tumble?

Cora whispered, barely a breath, “Did we not stack it quite right? Did her apple choice make our beautiful pyramid feel not so beautiful anymore?” They looked at the slightly tilted apples, the gentle leanings, and a little worry, small and soft as a fallen leaf, sat in their tummies. Coach Pansy happily munched, a soft smile, but the pyramid looked a little unsure of itself, a little shy.

The very next day they decided to build an even more perfect pyramid, one that would not wobble at all, firm as the oldest oak. They stacked extra carefully, pressing each apple with all their might. But somehow, as they looked, it did not feel as lovely. Too stiff, too tight, too serious. It did not have the graceful friendly feel of their usual happy pyramids. They sighed, a gentle squirrel sound that barely stirred the air.

Coach Pansy arrived again, ears perked with amusement, eyes twinkling. She saw the tense stillness of the new pyramid and smiled a knowing smile. “An apple pyramid is not just about being straight and tall and perfectly aligned. It is about the joy it brings to the heart. I chose that apple from the middle because it was the perfect colour for my afternoon tea, a shade that reminded me of the sunset. Your pyramids are indeed lovely, but sometimes just one special apple, chosen for a special reason, is what makes someone’s day.”

They looked at each other, eyes wide. Her words were like a warm ray chasing the little worry, melting it like snow in spring. Not the perfect shape. Making someone happy. Picking the apple that was just right for them, for that moment.

“So,” said Maple, tail a happy flick, “maybe we can make a special apple just for you. An apple that whispers your name!” Cora nodded, eyes bright, tail twitching with a new kind of thoughtful excitement. They found the most rosy plump apple, the very one Coach Pansy would love, glowing with happiness. Instead of putting it in a big pyramid, they placed it carefully on a soft green leaf, right at the front of the stand, like a little gift. When Coach Pansy saw it, her eyes twinkled even more. “Thank you. This is just perfect. It feels like a little piece of sunshine.”

From that day on they still loved their apple pyramids, for they brought order and beauty to the stand. They also remembered Coach Pansy’s words about joy and specialness. Every apple was special, and sometimes the most beautiful arrangement was the one that brought a quiet smile or a happy sigh to just one friend. Twilight painted the sky in sleepy colours. The first stars peeked, tiny diamonds on dark velvet. They felt warm and peaceful, knowing their work, in its own gentle way, made the world a little sweeter.

Cora logged middle-row wobble / stiff-oak stack / leaf-gift in the stand book, left Mr. Thistlewick his pyramids still allowed to be pyramids, and let Maple keep the dandelion-puff tail busy choosing one apple that had a name. They snuggled in their cozy nest, ready for sweet dreams, the leaf out front already waiting for tomorrow’s tea.
